The best chain is QB11-QB12-QB7, with QB12 in the middle. I picked it from the current default calibration of the real garnet QPU (calibration set f81c45da-6e73-4b5d-a0fe-72c75635fade). That calibration lists 28 CZ pairs, and every pair has an IRB fidelity. The QB11-QB12 CZ has an IRB fidelity of 0.99869. The QB12-QB7 CZ has 0.99802. Their product is 0.99671, which is the highest of any connected 3-qubit chain. The next best chain is QB12-QB11-QB16, at 0.99469.

Next I built a 3-qubit GHZ circuit on exactly QB11, QB12 and QB7. The circuit puts QB12 into an equal mix of 0 and 1. Then it copies that state onto QB11 and onto QB7. Each copy is a CNOT made from a CZ on pair QB12-QB11 or QB12-QB7, placed between two single-qubit rotations. No other two-qubit gates are used. All 3 qubits are measured. I checked the circuit with a local simulation first. It gives 000 and 111 with 50% each, which is the ideal GHZ result.

I ran it on garnet:mock with 200 shots (job 01a16041-1a3a-740d-b51a-d34f517e3f2b). The job completed. The counts are 000: 55, 111: 57, 100: 41 and 011: 47. Each bitstring reads QB11, QB12, QB7 from left to right.

The mock does not simulate the circuit. It returns random bits, so these counts do not show a GHZ state. The 100 and 011 results would be rare on a real or ideal device. The mock run shows that the server accepted the circuit on those exact qubits and gates. A real garnet run should give mostly 000 and 111.

The principle is entanglement. In a GHZ state, the three qubits are never 0 or 1 on their own before you measure. When you measure, all three agree: they come out all 0 or all 1. Every CZ gate adds a small error, so the chain whose two CZ gates are most reliable gives the cleanest GHZ state. The product of the two fidelities is a rough estimate of how well both gates together work.
